summary.text: For consecutive divisors \(a<b\), the condition that \(b\) is odd and \(b\ge 2a\) is equivalent to \(b>2a\): equality is impossible for odd \(b\), while if a jump had even \(b\), then \(b/2\) would be a divisor strictly between \(a\) and \(b\). Thus the counted pairs are exactly the breaks in the sorted divisor list, and one plus their number is the number of maximal blocks in which adjacent terms grow by at most a factor of \(2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\ge 1\), and write the positive divisors of \(n\) in strictly increasing order as
\[
1=d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_r=n.
\]
The list is nonempty because \(1\mid n\).

We use the arithmetic characterization of A237271 associated with the symmetric representation of \(\sigma(n)\):
\[
a(n)
 =1+\#\bigl\{i\in\{1,\ldots,r-1\}:
 d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr\}.
\tag{1}
\]
Thus it remains to compare the adjacent pairs counted in (1) with the breaks between maximal \(2\)-dense sublists.

A contiguous sublist of the ordered divisor list is \(2\)-dense precisely when each adjacent pair within it satisfies
\[
d_{i+1}\le 2d_i.
\]
Accordingly, a break occurs between \(d_i\) and \(d_{i+1}\) precisely when
\[
d_{i+1}>2d_i.
\tag{2}
\]
Cutting the ordered divisor list at every such break produces contiguous blocks. Every adjacent pair within any one block satisfies the required inequality, so each block is \(2\)-dense. Moreover, each block is maximal: if it could be extended across one of its endpoints, it would cross a place where (2) holds, and the enlarged block would fail to be \(2\)-dense. Conversely, every maximal \(2\)-dense contiguous sublist must be one of these blocks, because it cannot cross a break, while omitting neighboring terms without a break would contradict maximality. Therefore
\[
\#\{\text{maximal \(2\)-dense sublists}\}
 =1+\#\bigl\{i:d_{i+1}>2d_i\bigr\}.
\tag{3}
\]
This formula also covers the case \(r=1\): there are no adjacent pairs or breaks, and the sole divisor forms one maximal block.

We now prove the key local equivalence. For each pair of consecutive divisors \(d_i,d_{i+1}\),
\[
\bigl(d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 d_{i+1}>2d_i.
\tag{4}
\]

First suppose that \(d_{i+1}\) is odd and \(d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\). Equality cannot hold, because \(2d_i\) is even whereas \(d_{i+1}\) is odd. Hence the inequality is strict, giving \(d_{i+1}>2d_i\).

Conversely, suppose that
\[
d_{i+1}>2d_i.
\]
The weak inequality \(d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\) follows immediately. It remains to show that \(d_{i+1}\) is odd. Assume for contradiction that it is even. Then for some positive integer \(e\),
\[
d_{i+1}=2e.
\]
Since \(d_{i+1}\mid n\) and \(e\mid d_{i+1}\), transitivity of divisibility gives \(e\mid n\). On the other hand,
\[
2d_i<d_{i+1}=2e
\]
implies \(d_i<e\), while \(e<2e=d_{i+1}\). Thus \(e\) is a divisor of \(n\) lying strictly between \(d_i\) and \(d_{i+1}\). This contradicts the fact that these are consecutive terms in the increasing list of all divisors of \(n\). Therefore \(d_{i+1}\) must be odd, proving (4).

By (4), the set of indices counted in the arithmetic characterization (1) is exactly the set of breaks counted in (3). Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=1+\#\bigl\{i:
 d_{i+1}\text{ is odd and }d_{i+1}\ge 2d_i\bigr\}\\
&=1+\#\bigl\{i:d_{i+1}>2d_i\bigr\}\\
&=\#\{\text{maximal contiguous \(2\)-dense sublists of the divisors of \(n\)}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, for every \(n\ge1\), the number of parts in the symmetric representation of \(\sigma(n)\), namely \(a(n)\), is the number of maximal sublists of the ordered divisors of \(n\) in which consecutive terms increase by a factor of at most \(2\).
